brief.theme: A bottom-up way to redesign work with AI: map tasks, track change, decide who does each better, orchestrate hand-offs, iterate
brief.thesis: Beyond top-down debates about occupations, the practical path is bottom-up: map every task, watch it change, assign each to whoever does it better, and keep iterating on the hand-offs between people and agents

messages.text: Map every task and watch how it changes
Decide task by task whether a person or an agent does it better, then orchestrate
New problems live in the hand-offs, so iterate: upskill for human tasks, engineer harnesses and governance for agent tasks

brief.closingQuestion: What if we built teams around flows of tasks that people and agents keep improving together?

onScreen.headline: Apple is hiring to build its own AI agent

narration.text: This week, Bloomberg reported that Apple is hiring to build its own AI agent. One designed to browse the web, control apps, and write code on your behalf. A race OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta are already in. And inside every company, the same conversation starts again.

onScreen.headline: Start with the tasks, not the org chart
onScreen.body: A job is a bundle of tasks. AI takes tasks, one at a time.

narration.text: It's almost always top-down. Which occupations will AI be better at? Which areas should we redesign first? What should the new org chart look like? Those discussions will happen. But there's another way to look at it, from the bottom up. Forget the job title for a moment. Start with the tasks. Because a job is a bundle of tasks, and AI doesn't take the bundle. It takes tasks, one at a time.

onScreen.label: tasks workers do that the official US catalog doesn't list
onScreen.context: Step 1 · Map every task · 132 workers, 6 occupations

narration.text: Step one. Map every task. Sounds obvious, but the official maps are already out of date. In October, a Stanford team used an AI interviewer to talk with 132 workers in six occupations. They found 79 tasks people actually do that have no match in the official US task catalog. A few of them only exist because of AI. Real work, with no name yet.

steps.label: Track
steps.text: New tasks in, old ones out

narration.text: Step two. Watch how the tasks change. Because that study used an AI interviewer, a map like this could be redrawn often, not once every few years. New tasks appear. Others fade away. The job title stays the same, while the work underneath it keeps moving. A task map is not a document. It's a living thing.

onScreen.label: less time than professionals, but weaker work and some made-up data
onScreen.context: Step 3 · Who does each task better?

narration.text: Step three. For each task, ask who does it better. Late last year, researchers at Carnegie Mellon and Stanford gave the same work to professionals and to AI agents. The agents took 88.3% less time and cost 90.4 to 96.2% less. But their work was weaker, and some of them covered the gaps by making up data. So the answer is never everything to the agent. It's task by task.

Step four. Orchestrate. Here is a consultant's week, task by task. She is better at interviewing people, framing the problem, and persuading a room. The agent is better at gathering data, benchmarking, building the model, and drafting slides. The work alternates between them, and because the agent's tasks finish faster, the whole flow does too. In customer service, it's the same shape. The human reads the mood and handles the exception. The agent checks identity, pulls the history, and processes the refund.

onScreen.label: faster with AI as a helper, slower when handing over whole tasks
onScreen.context: New problems live in the hand-offs

narration.text: And this is where new problems show up. In the hand-offs. The same study found that when people used AI as a helper inside their own process, they worked 24.3% faster. When they handed whole tasks to AI, they got 17.7% slower, busy verifying and debugging.

onScreen.label: (A$440,000) contract. Fake references reached the client.
onScreen.context: New problems live in the hand-offs

narration.text: And in 2025, Deloitte delivered a report to the Australian government, a contract worth about 290,000 US dollars. It had references that didn't exist and a made-up court quote. The corrected version disclosed that generative AI had been used, and Deloitte agreed to refund part of the fee. The errors made it all the way to the client.

onScreen.label: more cancers found, no more false positives, 44% less reading work

narration.text: Now look at a hand-off that was designed and tested. In Sweden, a trial with more than 100,000 women gave AI the first read in breast cancer screening. It sorted the mammograms by risk and flagged suspicious spots. Radiologists stayed in charge of the decisions. The result. 29% more cancers found, with no increase in false positives, and 44% less reading work for the radiologists. Same technology. A different hand-off.

onScreen.headline: Different paths. One loop.
onScreen.body: Upskill people for human tasks. Engineer agents for theirs. Give every hand-off an owner.

narration.text: So the work never ends with the first design. You run the flow, you see where it breaks, and you fix it. Again and again. And each side improves in its own way. For the human tasks, upskilling focused on what people do best. Framing, judgment, empathy, persuasion, and checking what AI produces. For the agent tasks, engineering. Better harnesses, guardrails, evaluation and governance. And for every hand-off, a clear owner.

onScreen.headline: What if teams were built around that loop?
onScreen.body: Not job titles. Flows of tasks people and agents keep improving, every week.

narration.text: Which makes me wonder. What if we built teams, and maybe whole organizations, around that loop? Not around job titles, but around flows of tasks that people and agents keep improving together, every week. What would your team look like?

onScreen.question: Which of your tasks would you hand to an agent tomorrow?

narration.text: Follow along for a new episode every week. This was What's just now possible?
